question: What does a flight director show the pilot?

options.text: Raw deviation from the localizer and glide slope only
The aircraft's attitude without any commands
The autopilot's servo positions
Computed steering commands to fly a chosen path

explanation: The flight director computes the pitch and roll needed to achieve the selected mode and shows them as command bars. The pilot, or the autopilot, follows them.

question: What does the abbreviation CWS stand for in automatic flight?

options.text: Control wheel steering
Central warning system
Course width selector
Computed wind speed

explanation: Control wheel steering lets the pilot manoeuvre through the autopilot by moving the control wheel, the autopilot holding the new attitude when it is released.

question: What is N1 on a high-bypass turbofan?

options.text: The rpm of the high-pressure spool, shown in revolutions per minute
The first stage turbine temperature
The rpm of the first compressor stage, the fan, as a percentage
The engine pressure ratio

explanation: N1 is the speed of the first stage of compression, normally the fan on a high-bypass engine, shown as a percentage.

question: In autoland terminology, what does LAND 3 indicate?

options.text: A single-channel system with monitoring
A fail-operational system
A system for CAT I only
A fail-passive system

explanation: LAND 3 is fail-operational and LAND 2 is fail-passive, reflecting the number of autopilot channels engaged and monitoring.

question: What is the flight mode annunciator?

options.text: A light that shows the flight director has failed and must be switched off
An aural call of the active mode
The part of the PFD showing FD, autopilot and autothrottle modes
The control panel used to select the modes

explanation: The FMA is the area of the primary flight display that annunciates the flight director, autopilot and autothrottle modes and status.

question: What is normally shown around the EADI on a primary flight display?

options.text: Engine and fuel indications
The navigation map and the active route
The weather radar picture
Speed, altitude and vertical speed tapes

explanation: The PFD brings all the information needed to fly onto one display: an EADI surrounded by speed, altitude and vertical speed tapes, often a compass, and the FMA.

question: What does the flight director computer do?

options.text: Stores the navigation database
Gathers and processes data and sends commands to the displays or autopilot
Supplies power to the display units
Measures attitude with its own internal gyros and accelerometers, like an IRS

explanation: All the information is gathered and processed in the FDC. Its outputs go to the symbol generators for the EADI and EHSI and/or to the autopilot.

question: An older aircraft refitted with modern displays still has analogue sensors. How are they connected?

options.text: Through an analogue-to-digital converter
They cannot be used at all
Directly to the digital symbol generators
Through the instrument amplifier only

explanation: Refitted aircraft may feed their analogue inputs through a converter to digital form so that modern displays and autopilots can use them.

question: Why is an instrument amplifier needed in an electromechanical flight director?

options.text: To compare the two flight directors
To convert the analogue signals into a digital form
To generate symbols for the EADI
To amplify the signals enough to drive the display motors

explanation: Electromechanical instruments need amplified signals to drive their motors. On EFIS aircraft the FDC output goes straight to the symbol generators.

question: What is a remote vertical gyro?

options.text: An attitude gyro mounted away from the panel, driving the ADI
A gyro that measures yaw rate for the yaw damper
A standby attitude indicator with its own battery and gyro
A gyro in the ADI that can be removed

explanation: The vertical gyro that provides the attitude reference is not inside the panel instrument; it can be anywhere in the aircraft, normally near the CG, and drives the ADI display electrically.

question: What is one benefit of placing the vertical gyro near the aircraft's centre of gravity?

options.text: It removes the need for an erection system
It makes the ADI lighter and cheaper to replace
It gives a more accurate attitude reference
It allows the gyro to be air driven

explanation: Near the CG the gyro is less affected by accelerations from pitching and rolling, so the attitude is more accurate. Its electrical output can also feed the autopilot and other users.

question: In modern large aircraft, what usually replaces the vertical gyro as the attitude source?

options.text: The flux valve
The INS or IRS
The air data computer
A standby attitude indicator

explanation: More modern and larger aircraft use attitude from their INS or IRS, a more modern and much more sensitive version of a gyro.

question: What does the flight director mode controller allow the pilot to do?

options.text: Engage the autothrottle only
Select the display range of the ND
Change the FD mode, adjust pitch trim and switch it on or off
Select the radio frequencies and courses for the approach

explanation: The mode controller changes the FDS mode, alters the pitch trim of the command bars and switches the display on or off. On modern aircraft the MCP replaces it.

question: On a basic ILS mode annunciator, what does an amber LOC light show?

options.text: The localizer signal has failed
The localizer has been captured
The aircraft is past the localizer centreline
The localizer is armed, waiting for capture

explanation: An amber LOC light means the system is waiting to capture the localizer. It turns green when the localizer is captured.

question: On a basic mode annunciator, what does a green GS light show?

options.text: The glide slope is armed
The glide slope has been captured
The glide slope signal is unreliable
The aircraft is above the glide slope

explanation: Approaching the glide slope the GS light is amber (armed); it changes to green when the FDS has locked on to the glide slope.

question: On an FMA, how are engaged and armed modes shown?

options.text: Engaged green on the top line; armed white below
Engaged white on the top line; armed green below
Both green, the armed mode flashing
Engaged amber; armed magenta

explanation: Engaged modes are shown on the top line in green and armed modes on the line below in white. A newly changed mode is often surrounded by a box.

question: How is a newly changed mode emphasised on the FMA?

options.text: By a box drawn around it
By flashing the whole display
By an aural chime only
By showing it in red

explanation: Newly changed information on the FMA is often emphasised by a box around it for a short time.

question: What is "raw" information on a flight director display?

options.text: Data from the air data computer only, uncorrected
The command bar position
Information corrected for wind
Unprocessed deviation, such as the CDI bar

explanation: Raw information is not processed: the CDI bar and the glide slope pointer just show the aircraft left or right of track, or above or below the glide slope.

question: From what is the flight director's "computed" information derived?

options.text: The size of the deviation only, at that moment
The rate of change of deviation
The wind velocity from the INS
The pilot's control inputs

explanation: Computed information uses the rate of change of deviation so that the FD can command a turn onto track in good time rather than letting the aircraft fly through it.

question: If the flight director system fails, which information may still be usable?

options.text: The pitch trim setting of the command bars
The gain scheduling
The raw deviation information
The computed command bars

explanation: When the FDS fails its computed commands are lost, but the raw information, such as the CDI bar and glide slope pointer, may still be available and used.

question: Does the flight director need wind data to correct for drift when tracking a course?

options.text: Yes; it needs a wind input from the INS to work out the drift
No; flying the desired track corrects for drift itself
No; it ignores drift altogether
Yes; it needs the forecast wind entered

explanation: The FD compares actual track with desired track and commands whatever is needed to fly the desired track, so drift is compensated without wind information.

question: On an electromechanical ADI, what does a "GYRO" flag indicate?

options.text: The vertical reference or its power has failed
The flight director computer itself has failed
The compass is in DG mode
The glide slope signal is unreliable

explanation: A GYRO flag appears if the vertical gyro or other vertical reference, or its power supply, fails.

question: Which flag shows a failure of the flight director computer, the instrument amplifier or the ADI itself?

options.text: NAV
GYRO only
ATT or FD
GS

explanation: Failures of the FDC, the instrument amplifier or the ADI are shown by a flag labelled ATT or FD, normally on the ADI.

question: Where does the GS flag appear when the glide slope is unreliable?

options.text: Over the command bars
In the centre of the HSI compass card
On the mode control panel
In front of the raw glide slope scale

explanation: The GS flag appears in front of the raw glide slope scale, beside the ADI or on the HSI.

question: What does a NAV flag on the HSI indicate?

options.text: The flight director is switched off at its control panel
A failure of the vertical gyro
A failure of the compass gyro
Poor or lost VOR, LNAV or LOC information

explanation: Poor reception or loss of VOR, LNAV or localizer information is shown by a NAV flag, normally on the HSI.

question: What may the HSI show if the magnetic reference of the compass is lost?

options.text: A NAV flag on the HSI
That the compass is in DG mode
A GYRO flag on the attitude indicator
A GS flag on the HSI

explanation: The HSI indicates when the compass system is working in directional gyro (DG) mode, with no magnetic reference, as well as a power failure flag.

question: How can the pilot offset the FD command bars to hold a chosen pitch attitude?

options.text: With the autopilot disconnect switch
With the course selector
With the pitch trim knob or wheel
With the heading select knob

explanation: The pitch trim knob or wheel moves the command bars vertically to give an aiming point for a constant pitch angle in level flight, climb or descent.

question: When is the FD pitch trim inhibited?

options.text: Whenever any other pitch mode is active
Below 400 ft radio altitude only
When heading mode is selected
Whenever the autopilot is disengaged in flight

explanation: The pitch trim system works only when no other pitch mode is active; once a mode such as altitude hold is engaged, the trim is inhibited.

question: How is the flight director take-off mode engaged?

options.text: By switching on the FD at 80 kt
By rotating the pitch trim wheel fully nose-up
By pressing a TO/GA switch on the thrust levers
By selecting LNAV on the MCP

explanation: With both FD switches on before the take-off roll, pressing either TO/GA switch on the thrust levers engages the take-off mode, annunciated TO/GA.

question: In a typical system, what are the initial FD take-off commands?

options.text: 15° nose-up and wings level
10° nose-down and wings level
5° nose-up and 5° bank
Level pitch and the runway heading

explanation: In the system described, the initial commands are 10° nose-down and wings level; at 60 kt IAS they change to 15° nose-up and wings level.

question: In a typical system, at what speed do the FD take-off pitch commands change to 15° nose-up?

options.text: 60 kt IAS
80 kt IAS
V1
VR

explanation: The commands change from 10° nose-down to 15° nose-up, wings level, at 60 kt IAS.

question: If the FD switches are off, how can the bars still be brought up during the take-off?

options.text: Switch on the FD before 60 kt only; it cannot be done later
Select LVL CHG after lift-off
Engage the autopilot on the runway
Press TO/GA after 80 kt, within 2000 ft or 150 s of lift-off

explanation: Pressing TO/GA after 80 kt IAS but before 2000 ft or 150 seconds after lift-off makes the command bars appear automatically.

question: After lift-off with sufficient climb rate, what speed does the FD command in take-off mode?

options.text: 250 kt
V2 exactly
The MCP speed minus 10 kt
The MCP speed plus 20 kt

explanation: Once a sufficient climb rate is reached, the FD commands pitch to hold the MCP speed (set preflight to V2) plus 20 kt.

question: Below 400 ft RA, how is the FD take-off mode ended?

options.text: By pressing TO/GA again
By turning off both FD switches
By engaging an autopilot
By selecting another pitch mode

explanation: Below 400 ft RA the take-off mode can only be terminated by turning off both FD switches. Above 400 ft another pitch mode or an autopilot can end it.

question: Engaging the autopilot after an FD take-off, with no other mode selected, gives which modes?

options.text: ALT HOLD for pitch and HDG SEL for roll
VNAV for pitch and LNAV for roll
LVL CHG for pitch and HDG SEL for roll
V/S for pitch and LOC for roll

explanation: The autopilot and FD engage in level change for pitch and heading select for roll, unless a different roll mode had already been chosen.

question: An engine fails during the take-off before V2. What speed do the FD pitch commands use?

options.text: V2
V2 + 20 kt
The MCP speed minus 20 kt
The speed at the failure

explanation: Before V2 the reference is V2. Between V2 and V2 + 20 kt it is the speed at failure, and at or above V2 + 20 kt it is V2 + 20 kt; never below V2.

question: An engine fails at V2 + 10 kt during the FD take-off. What speed is commanded?

options.text: V2 + 20 kt
The MCP selected speed plus 20 kt
V2
The speed at which the engine failed

explanation: For a failure after V2 but below V2 + 20 kt, the reference speed is the speed at which the failure occurred.

question: An engine fails at V2 + 30 kt during the FD take-off. What speed is commanded?

options.text: The best rate of climb speed
V2 + 20 kt
V2
V2 + 30 kt

explanation: For a failure at or above V2 + 20 kt, the commanded speed is V2 + 20 kt.

question: After an engine failure in FD take-off mode, how does the roll command change?

options.text: Roll commands are removed
It commands 15° of bank
It stays the same as with all engines operating
It commands a turn towards the side of the live engine

explanation: Roll control remains as for all engines operating: wings level through the take-off climb-out.

question: In altitude hold, what do the FD command bars show if the aircraft climbs above the selected level?

options.text: A pitch-down command
A pitch-up command
A roll command
No change; they stay central

explanation: At the selected level the bars are neutral. Above it they command pitch down, and below it pitch up, using ADC signals.

question: What does the FD do in heading mode?

options.text: Holds the current track over the ground until a new one is set
Tracks the selected VOR radial
Holds the heading at engagement only
Commands a turn onto the selected heading and holds it

explanation: The pilot selects a heading on the HSI, FD panel or MCP, and the FD gives fly-to commands to reach and hold it.

question: In VOR/LOC mode, what must be done before the FD will intercept a VOR radial?

options.text: Select heading mode on the HSI course knob
Tune and identify the VOR and set the course
Enter the wind into the FMS
Engage the autopilot in CWS

explanation: After tuning and identifying the station, selecting VOR/LOC and setting the desired course, the FDS commands the intercept and then holds the track.

question: In heading select, the selected heading is changed by 90°. How does the FD roll bar behave?

options.text: It moves right and stays until wings level
It moves fully right and stays there until within 30° of the heading
It moves right, then centres as the deviation reduces
It disappears until the new heading is reached

explanation: The roll command is proportional to the heading error, up to a bank limit, so the bar moves to command the turn and progressively returns to centre as the heading nears the selection.

question: The FD command bars are above and to the left of the aircraft symbol. What are they commanding?

options.text: Pitch up and turn left
Pitch up and turn right
Pitch down and turn left
Pitch down and turn right

explanation: The bars show where to fly the aircraft symbol: raise the nose and bank left until the symbol meets the bars.

question: When turning to intercept a radial, what do the FD bars indicate?

options.text: The correct attitude to intercept it
A fixed 30° bank
A fixed 15° bank
The raw deviation from the radial, uncorrected

explanation: The FD computes the attitude needed for a smooth intercept, from the deviation and its rate of change, and shows that as the command.

question: For a flight director ILS approach, what is set in the course window?

options.text: The runway length
The decision height
The inbound approach course
The glide slope angle in degrees

explanation: The ILS is tuned and identified and the approach course (the inbound magnetic course) is set in the course window, then APP is selected.

question: During an FD approach, what does the FD command at glide slope capture?

options.text: A turn onto the localizer centreline
A pitch-down to follow the glide slope
A pitch-up to level off
A go-around

explanation: When the glide slope is captured the annunciator changes and the FD commands nose-down pitch to fly the glide slope.

question: On older systems, what could MAN/GS mode be used for?

options.text: To disconnect the autopilot at decision height
To fly a manual go-around
To fly the approach without a localizer
To force a glide slope capture from above

explanation: If established on the localizer above the glide slope, MAN/GS forces the FDS to accept a capture from above. It can also set a fixed intercept angle or force a capture if the beam-sensing circuits fail.

question: How may a modern system capture the glide slope from above?

options.text: By disconnecting the approach mode
It cannot; the crew must go around
By increasing the rate of descent automatically
By commanding a climb back to the intercept altitude

explanation: Modern systems may adjust automatically and capture from above by increasing the rate of descent.

question: In the system described, which conditions allow FD go-around mode to engage?

options.text: In flight below 2000 ft RA, not in TO mode, TO/GA pressed
Above 2000 ft RA, with APP mode active
On the ground, with both FD switches on
Below 400 ft RA, with the autopilot engaged in CMD and APP armed

explanation: The aircraft must be in flight below 2000 ft RA and not in take-off mode, and a TO/GA switch must be pressed. The FD switches may be on or off.

question: For an all-engines FD go-around, what is the initial pitch command?

options.text: 13° nose-up
15° nose-up
10° nose-up
20° nose-up

explanation: For a two-engine go-around the FD commands 15° nose-up and holds the approach ground track. After a set climb rate it holds the manoeuvring speed for the flap setting.

question: For a single-engine FD go-around, what is the initial pitch command?

options.text: 15° nose-up
8° nose-up
10° nose-up
13° nose-up

explanation: With one engine the initial pitch command is 13° nose-up; as climb rate builds the FD holds a target speed.

question: In an FD go-around, which roll command is given?

options.text: Hold the runway heading set on the MCP
Hold the approach ground track
Wings level, with no track hold
Turn onto the missed approach heading

explanation: The roll command holds the ground track at the time of engagement, the same for one or two engines.

question: Below 400 ft RA, how is the FD go-around mode ended?

options.text: By engaging an autopilot
By pressing TO/GA again
By selecting a new roll mode on the MCP
By turning both FD switches off

explanation: Below 400 ft RA both FD switches must be turned from on to off to leave the go-around mode. Above 400 ft other pitch and roll modes can be selected.

question: In FD go-around above 400 ft, the pitch mode is changed first. What happens to the roll mode?

options.text: It changes to wings level
It changes to LNAV automatically, if a route is active
It changes to HDG SEL automatically
It stays in go-around

explanation: If the pitch mode is changed first, the roll mode automatically changes to heading select. If the roll mode is changed first, pitch stays in go-around.

question: An engine fails 5 seconds after FD go-around engagement. What is the target speed?

options.text: The MCP selected approach speed
V2 + 20 kt
The speed at the engine failure
The speed at go-around engagement

explanation: Within 10 seconds of engagement the MCP approach speed becomes the target. After 10 seconds it depends on how the speed compares with the engagement speed.

question: An engine fails 15 seconds after FD go-around engagement, 10 kt above the engagement speed. What is the target speed?

options.text: The speed at go-around engagement
The MCP selected approach speed
V2
The current airspeed

explanation: After 10 seconds, if the speed at failure is more than 5 kt above the engagement speed, the current airspeed becomes the target; if within 5 kt, the engagement speed does.

question: What is the lowest go-around target speed the FD will command, outside windshear?

options.text: VREF minus 10 kt
V2 for the flap setting
The approach speed minus 5 kt
The stall speed

explanation: In all cases the go-around target is not less than V2 for the flap position, except in windshear.

question: How does a modern flight director computer avoid commanding an overstressing manoeuvre?

options.text: It limits all bank angles to 10°
It hands control to the autopilot
It holds the aircraft's limits in memory and uses ADC data
It uses the pilot's control forces as its main limiting input

explanation: The FDC is configured for the aircraft type and stores its performance limits; with ADC inputs it never commands a manoeuvre that would overstress the aircraft.

question: What is gain scheduling in a flight director?

options.text: Varying the size of the commands to suit the phase
Switching between the two flight directors as the approach goes on
Changing the display brightness with time
Selecting a new mode at a set time

explanation: Gain scheduling varies the gain of the pitch and roll demands with the task. On an approach the glide slope commands are reduced as the aircraft nears the runway.

question: Why must glide slope commands be reduced as an ILS approach progresses?

options.text: The localizer becomes wider close in
An angular error means less height error close in
The glide slope signal becomes weaker as the aircraft gets close in
The aircraft is slower close in

explanation: The beams converge towards the runway. One degree of error is about 608 ft at 6 NM but about 54 ft at ½ NM, so the same indication needs a gentler correction close in.

question: About how much vertical distance does 1° of glide slope error represent at 6 NM?

options.text: About 608 ft
About 318 ft
About 1200 ft
About 54 ft

explanation: 1° in 60 is about 1 in 60, so at 6 NM (≈36 500 ft) the height is about 6 × 6080 / 60 ≈ 608 ft. At ½ NM it is about 54 ft.

question: How did the earliest systems decide when to reduce flight director gain on an approach?

options.text: By the DME distance
By the radio altimeter height above the runway
By the marker beacons
By time, for example 45 s after glide slope capture

explanation: Early systems used time, reducing the gain about 45 seconds after glide slope capture. Later systems used marker beacons, then the radio altimeter.

question: Why has gain scheduling by marker beacons fallen out of use?

options.text: The beacons cannot be received by the aircraft below about 200 ft
The beacons interfere with the localizer
Many airfields no longer have marker beacons
The beacons are too far from the runway

explanation: Marker beacons matched the scheduling to the approach, but many airfields have removed them, so the method has fallen into disuse.

question: Why is the radio altimeter a good source for gain scheduling?

options.text: It measures the glide slope angle
It gives the distance to the runway threshold directly, from the ground station
It works only above 2500 ft
It needs no ground signal and gives smooth, height-based scheduling

explanation: The radio altimeter relies on no ground signals and gives scheduling related to actual height, phased in gradually rather than in steps.

question: What does the FD comparator do?

options.text: Switches the autopilot over to the other flight director
Removes the bars if the two FDs disagree
Selects the more accurate FD
Averages the two FD commands

explanation: With two FDs, the comparator monitors the command bars and removes them if the two disagree by about 1–4° of pitch or 3–9° of roll. The bars return when the difference is within limits.

question: Under which conditions does FD comparison operate?

options.text: Only on the ground before take-off
Whenever either FD is switched on, at any height and in any mode
Both FDs on, no autopilot, TO/GA or APP below 800 ft RA
Only above 2500 ft radio altitude

explanation: Both FD switches must be on with neither autopilot engaged, and the comparison runs only in TO/GA or APP mode below 800 ft RA.

question: When is FD comparison inhibited?

options.text: On the ground, on bus transfer, or after an FD or sensor failure
During the take-off roll above 80 kt
Whenever the autothrottle is engaged in any mode during the flight
In the cruise above FL100 only

explanation: It is inhibited on the ground, when either FD is affected by an electrical bus transfer, and when either an FD sensor or an FD fails.

question: If one flight director computer fails, how can both pilots keep FD displays?

options.text: The autopilot drives the displays
Both sides can be driven from the remaining FDC
The standby attitude indicator shows the commands for both pilots
Each pilot reverts to raw data only

explanation: A switch can feed the output of the serviceable FDC to both sets of ADIs and HSIs, as long as the display equipment is serviceable. EFIS aircraft also have a spare symbol generator.
